meta.title: Pyreon: your component runs once
meta.description: A signal-based TypeScript framework. Components run once, only the DOM node that changed updates. A quarter of React's JavaScript for the same app. Full stack on the web, with iOS and Android from the same .tsx (experimental).

share.title: Your component runs once. Ever.
share.sub: A quarter of React's JavaScript. 2.6× faster at 10,000 rows.

sections.title: Your component runs once. Ever.
sections.lede: Pyreon updates the one DOM node that changed, so there is nothing to memoise and nothing re-renders. Full stack on the web today, and the same `.tsx` compiles to SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose (experimental).

status.text: iOS and Android: experimental (we mean it)

sections.title: No re-renders. Just updates.
sections.lede: Your component function runs one time. When a signal changes, Pyreon writes to the exact text node or attribute that reads it. Click the counter: the component never runs again.

counter.spec: Real @pyreon/core counter. Each click increments 'text node writes' and pulses the number (brand signal pulse, 200 ms). 'component runs' stays 1.

sections.title: Delete useMemo. Delete useCallback. Delete every dependency array.
sections.lede: React re-runs your component on every change, so you write code to stop it. Pyreon never re-runs it, so that code has nothing left to do.

sections.title: One .tsx file. A website, an iPhone app and an Android app.
sections.lede: Build the website now. The same components compile to real SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose views, tested on an iOS Simulator and an Android emulator in CI. Experimental, and labelled that way on every page.
points: Primitives that render DOM on the web and native views on the phone (22 in the next release)

Web-first packages say so per package, so nothing surprises you on device

sections.title: Your AI writes a bug. The framework catches it.
sections.lede: Assistants learned on React, and some React habits compile fine in a signals framework and then never update. Pyreon ships the tools that catch them while the code is written.

items.name: MCP server
items.text: 24 tools. `get_api` returns the real API, `validate` flags misuse with the line, the offending code and the fix. No network calls.

items.name: Reactivity Lens
items.text: `live` and `static` hints in your editor, on every expression, as you type.

items.name: pyreon check
items.text: Scans changed files, prints each finding with its fix, `--fix` applies the auto-fixable ones, exits non-zero in CI.

items.name: 133 lint rules
items.text: In 25 categories, from destructured props and context to browser globals in server code.

example.finding: props-destructured-body · 2:8 · read props.label so it stays reactive

sections.title: Built for teams who'd rather ship than glue.
sections.lede: If your package.json has thirty libraries that each solve a tenth of the problem, this is for you.

items.title: SaaS and dashboards
items.text: Forms, validation, query, tables and charts that already know each other, on one version. Skip the week of wiring libraries together.

items.title: Content and marketing sites
items.text: Every route picks SSG, ISR or SSR. Markdown collections and RSS are built in, with scheduled posts in the next release. This site and its blog run on it.

items.title: A web app that wants a phone app
items.text: Ship the web version now. Screens built from the primitives compile to SwiftUI and Compose as native support fills in. No second team.

items.title: Teams leaving React
items.text: Run your React components on react-compat, then convert one component at a time. Your AI assistant gets the real API through MCP.

sections.title: 40 products. One version.
sections.lede: One reactive core, one release train, one set of docs. Here are the ones people start with.

sections.title: Bring your React app.
sections.lede: Compat layers with near-full public-API parity for React, Vue, Solid, Svelte and Preact. Point your build at the layer, keep shipping, and move a component to signals when you choose, not when a deadline says so.

sections.title: What's ready, and what isn't (yet).
sections.lede: Pre-1.0 means versions can still break, and we say so in a changeset when they do. The web is what apps run on today. iOS and Android are experimental and move every release.

cd examples/benchmark && bun bench-fair.ts --repeat 5 --wait-quiet 4
